Not a professional, but a student like you, so this is what I've been told.

Get a job in the field. Could be helpdesk, could be systems engineering, just get experience. Companies value experience over any sort of certification, whether it be a degree or a certificate. Most places look for 3-5 years experience with maybe a specialization or two. Don't feel the need to be a master in everything, like you said, IT is huge.

I'm currently a student worker at my school where I'm going for a BA in Computer Science. The only thing the BA is going to give me is a foot in the door if I ever consider management (god forbid). I've been working at the IT department for two years. I work with people who have been in the field for longer than I've been alive and they are still learning things every day.

Bottom line, just get experience and you'll be fine. Having ambition doesn't hurt, just be careful about what you say you can do and what you can actually do.

Networking means you're learning python. Go through the tutorial, then visit the Internet Protocols section of the library reference and just play around. Get comfortable at coding servers.

Book knowledge is nice for taking tests. Actually knowing what the fuck you're doing is what makes for successful interviews.

You don't have to know a programming language in order to get into IT, but it can help.

If you're on the admin/ops side of things, it helps you understand the systems you're running, and helps you build automated approaches to solving problems when the tools don't do exactly what you want.

As a hiring manager, I don't want someone who just knows how to use tools, if you understand the systems, you can learn a tool quickly. I want someone who can reason solutions. I want someone who can recognize a good Google answer from a bad one without having to try them all, and I want someone who can work from a partial answer and infer a good one.

That takes system understanding and a certain approach to problem solving... both thing that can be greatly enhanced by being proficient in at least one language

To expand slightly though, it's not strictly necessary.

I work with many IT folks who don't know any programming. They project manage, they do help desk work, they interface with other departments, they do sysadmin work, they manage teams, they direct organizations, etc.

You're just a bit more limited in your growth down some of those paths. But it's still an open world
Bachelors in Applied Computer Science here. Most companies will not care about the "applied": they want to see 1) a degree 2) portfolio/github and 3) previous experience. Don't sweat it too much.

Network professional here (wireless carrier space). As such, my answer will be directed as if you are asking specifically about this space. Asking about the IT industry as a whole is not going to get you many detailed answers. My day-to-day job includes virtually no programming as I mostly do network architecture. Your degree will certainly help land you a position at a company that looks for those sorts of things. If you are not getting any certifications in your studies, yu should definitely look into earning a few. Okay, here's the deal. If you're thinking your going to be a L337 programmer? Not happening. But, so long as you don't have such delusions, your fine. There are a lot of careers out there in IT that can use your degree. Project management, analysis, quality assurance, all juat as important as being a dev.

That being said, juat because there are roles out there doesnt equal a guarantee of employment. Wanting to work in IT is pretty broad. Do you want to do help desk, programming, networking, sys admin, etc? I started as a junior admin, and have been a sys admin/essentially whole IT department for over 10 years, so I'll explain what you'll need to know for that.

First, do you love IT, or are you just looking for a job that pays well? IT is not glamorous. 95% of the time your work will go unnoticed. I'm often reminded of Bender's conversation with God. http://static.tumblr.com/d97693085fdcd0dcdf05f23796b63242/k7s0wun/xNumps5fm/tumblr_static_tumblr_m2s8omomdf1qcmwsio1_500.gif When everything is running smoothly, people will think you don't do anything. You'll be blamed for your coworkers' mistakes and problems. If you do make a mistake, it can keep EVERYONE from being able to do their job. There is a lot of responsibility and trust in us. There's a lot of pressure. If you don't LOVE IT, it eat your soul.

Personally, I don't put a ton of faith in degrees and certs. I have both, but they really don't mean much to me. They are just to get your foot in the door or an interview. The real world is so drastically different than what you'll be taught. The books don't cover the legacy systems that you're taking over from the last guys poor decisions. The books don't cover PHBs or clueless users. The books cover an ideal world. This is great if you're started a company from the ground up. Most likely you won't be. I've seen new graduates just completely confused about how things are. You don't have everything documented? Why are you running this ancient software? Sometimes you don't have a choice. Yes, this legacy system sucks. I didn't choose it, and we're working on replacing it, but it's going to take years and tons of money, so this is what we have. Gutting running environments is hard work.

To be an admin, you'll need to know at least a bit of everything, but more importantly, you'll need drive and to continue learning and adapting as the playing field changes. I'd suggest looking for a Jr. admin job, and starting there. No matter what job or path you do follow, consistently ask for harder tasks and more responsibility. This may not affect your pay at your current job, but it will help with the next.

I've been in IT since 99, but on the application development side. I work in a major IT-centric city and have ridden the dot com bubble and collapse. We are currently host college interns in our department that have a lot of the same questions, so maybe I can help, even if you have more of an infrastructure/networking degree.

Your degree will certainly aid you in getting a job, but make no mistake, it only gives you a leg up to learn what it is all about. What you do and how successful you are once you get the job is entirely up to you.

Most of our infrastructure and networking team does know coding. The have to know how to adjust and tune the servers to run the applications. They have to be able to at least undertand what the code is trying to do.

Currently, for our group, it's C#, MVC and SQL. Conceptually, though, most of our developers can swap to a new coding language without much trouble.

For systems relates work, your degree is important, but IMO, it's more about the certifications you hold. You need to have specialized training to be really a valuable hire. Companies do not want to train, they want someone that knows their way around. An exception to this is if you can find a company that offers Jr lvl positions, but even there, you are going to have to noodle stuff out a lot on your own. They want people that can solve problems, not people that take orders. "Troubleshoot this" is a lot different the "let me show you how to troubleshoot this"

TL;DR: your degree gets your foot in the door. What you do after that is up to you.

I am a former net admin who is now a Sr. Sys Admin and I can probably shed light on a few things. Please take anything I say as merely advice and from my personal experience as it might not exactly apply to your in your area. Sorry for the wall of text, just thought I would share my experience as it might help you.

First off, I live in Houston Texas. There are a ton of IT jobs here so it has never been an issue for me finding jobs or interviews.

I started my IT career in the Military as a radio operator/System support specialist. I went to school for around 5 months learning switches, routers, general computer stuff and then eventually a bunch of tactical radio stuff. I had a very strong background in computers before hand so it made the school much easier for me. I was honor graduate and was lucky enough to take advantage of some extra classes at the end of my graduation, leading to a certification in Comptia A+. When I got to my unit I practically did nothing radio and was put into a helpdesk and Jr. Sys Admin role. I did this for about 2 years before deploying and getting my own company where I was the communications chief. I handled everything communication (servers, switches/routers/computers/phones/radios) for an infantry company of about 120 on a combat outpost. It was an extremely stressful time as I was put into an environment that was stable but had no documentation whatsoever. Aside from running missions as a radio operator every other day I did the general helpdesk and server/network maintenance throughout the day to day. I only mention this because I feel the experience is what really broke me into the IT field once I got out of the Army.

Straight out of the Army I landed a job with one of the biggest oil companies as a network admin. It was extremely proprietary and even though I had a good job, I was stagnating in a career that would get me no further in the IT world. I left after about a year and a half and got a job with a MSP. (Managed service provider - an IT company that does IT for other companies)

This MSP was based in another state and I took on their role as Regional Systems Admin for the Houston and South East region. It turns out that I was the only employee in the Houston and South East region which meant I handled all level 1-3 helpdesk, sys admin and net admin duties. They were in the healthcare market and I got an amazing amount of experience handling everything from Active Directory to Exchange to juniper firewalls and cisco switches and routers. I was again thrown head first into an environment that had me doing exactly what I wanted to do at a very uncomfortable rate. My clients were extremely cheap and had 15 year old equipment (side note- If you work for a MSP in the future, make sure you do your research. There are many MSPs that will take any client they can get in order to get that paycheck) This led to many many stressful days and nights.

I ended up leaving there after about a year to another MSP that I believed was a good fit. I didn't spend very long at this job because I found out very quick that the atmosphere of the company was toxic and there were many things going on that I didn't feel comfortable with. I will not go into details but I left here after 4 months. I was brought on as the Technical Team Lead for a MSP that handled clients in the financial industry. I was the point of contact for one of the biggest banks in Texas and even though the situation and job was shitty, I gained a great amount of knowledge and experience. At this point, I felt comfortable enough in my experience and skills to search for a more senior position and ended up getting another job offer a few days after putting my resume back out there.

This led to my current position as the Regional Sys Admin for an international shipping company. I handle all servers and many projects for the entire American region (north, central and south).

Now for my recommendations. You might have to suck it up and get an entry level position in the beginning. Even if its a 6 month internship or a shitty paying helpdesk job. You might be one of the lucky but I wouldn't count on it. I have applied for jobs and interviewed against quite a few fresh college graduates and I usually always get an offer. I am very thankful that I have been able to be picky as to who I want to work for because very many that I know have not been. During my time as a net admin I was chosen for a management position over someone with a year of experience and a bachelors and he rose quite a stink about it, bottom line is that good IT managers will balance their needs of an employee on experience, certifications and schooling. I do not have a bachelors (still going to school part time) but have a very diverse amount of experience and quite a few leading certifications. My latest interviewer hired me on the spot after about 20 minutes of interviewing and has since told me that the only people that had interviewed previously were college graduates that just did not have enough relevant experience. So basically the trend that I have seen in IT is that experience will get you hired, degrees will get you promoted.

As for your programming worries. I do not and have no interest in learning a program language. Every professional that I have worked around did not know a lick of programming that aided their jobs. (I know HTML but I am not going to count that) The only people, in my experience, that have programming knowledge that has directly influenced their jobs are developers. In my last job we had two in house devs that wrote the entire company scheme and directed the insides of the metrics system and other developer stuff that I have no idea about.

Sorry again for the wall of text, I hope that my experience might shed some light on the IT world and if you have any specific questions I would be more than happy to answer.

Don't sweat the degree. I was in the same spot thought my degree would prepare me for the work force, I was dead wrong. Think of it as a small window to many opportunities. Just finish school get a security + or network + cert you should be good to go.

Senior developer / hiring manager here. I don't care what is on your degree as long as you have the right buzzwords in your resume (which I only skim through to find the buzzwords I'm looking for) and then I will quiz you specifically on content related to those buzzwords. Also I will quiz you on some basic parsing and logic questions to make sure you're not a total idiot. I wouldn't waste time in Ruby yet, Python is still more popular, so you see more postings for it. A lot of shops are going to be C, C++, C# or Java or a mix of those, so C# is a decent choice if there are a lot of microsoft oriented shops around; where I am its all 4. Try and pick up more than two languages though, the more you know the more you can do.

I've spent 20 years in IT as a high school dropout with 3 attempts (and failures) at getting undergraduate degrees. I started out working for around $7 an hour as a half-assed tech, got a few certifications, crushed it at my first gig, and inside of 18 months in the field hit my first goal of making $50k/yr ($25/hr). Before I could even envision a goal of $100k/yr I was there, and the next time I looked up I was running an engineering team at a well-known Fortune-listed company before my mid-20s. From there I started building $billion datacenters because I really liked the precision of big rooms full of rack-mounted stuff and Internet networking made sense to me (Cricket Liu is still my favorite author), plus it didn't require me to actually be all that good at sysadmining.

Anyway, that's my background, and it's about as polar opposite as it can be from yours. In any case, here's some advice:

I feel like you have to know a programming language.

You really don't have to be able to program anything to be a good IT guy, and if you do decide to take up a tool, it doesn't have to be so dense as C# - you could do insanely well with a passable knowledge of python, or even realistically do insanely well without it either. If you pick up a language and find yourself loving it, then maybe you need to pursue a the path of the programmer. If not, then maybe you're a sysadmin, or a PM, or a security guy, or any one of a thousand other options. A few fields have hybrid expectations, such as web server admins usually needing a passable knowledge of PHP, but in those cases the level of mastery is well below that of a real coder.

Do you think that a Bachelors of Applied Science will get me anywhere?

Unless it's a graduate degree, the nature of your degree is essentially meaningless in the real world as it applies to your ability to advance once you get into the workforce; its existence is solely to get you your first job and to give you the absolute minimum of starting skills. Most of what you're learning won't be of nearly as much use as you think either. For instance, your concentration in Network won't put you on the front lines managing Cisco hardware in your first job, and even if that's where you eventually end up, what you learn in your degree concentration represents roughly .25% of what you'll need to know to run big routers for a living, and is the same .25% you'll learn in your first year on a lower-rung job anyway. The degree and its underlying knowledge should help you get that first job though, and keep you from having to hit the ground running so quickly as someone who didn't take the college route. By the end of year 1 or 2, however, you'll be equal in knowledge with everyone else with any other degree, and even with many people who skipped college, unless you're in a top-tier program. Your real advantage will be in the contacts you've made in school, any one of whom might someday land you a dream job, or join you at your own.

What's in demand? What advice can you give for someone aspiring to work in IT?

If in your first job you pay a lot of attention, learn every single iota of anything IT-related that anyone around you will teach you, take advantage of any paid training they offer (almost everyone has something), and have the most basic interpersonal skills (which it appears you do, plus you write well, which puts you in the 90th percentile), you'll do well in spite of yourself. Along the way you'll find one or two things that you really enjoy - maybe programming, maybe Novell (there's still money in the old shit), maybe networking or even getting into microcomputers and building brewery control systems or something equally obscure. Whatever it is, dive headfirst and get really good at whatever shiny thing grabs your attention and there's pretty much no way someone won't pay you to whack at it all day. Your focus might change over time too, so don't be afraid to let your old skills wind down if you're adding newer, more exciting ones to your repertoire as technology evolves.

My depression and anxiety disorders flare up all the time when I think about "what's next after college?"

A lot of IT people can empathize with you on this one, myself included. In many cases the very "crossed wires" which cause so many of us to experience these disorders are the same subconscious associations that allow for spectacular IT people. The IT world is huge, spans virtually every other industry on the planet, and still has an enormous amount of room for new innovations and ideas, so no matter what just know that even if the opportunity you seek today gets past you, there are still an absurd number of opportunities flying in right behind it.

You'll do great, just figure out what you love to do and do it until you're rich! Good luck!

Internships. I went to a pretty well regarded school, but honestly the core curriculum had some serious weak points. Where I really learned was through summer internships freshman through senior year. I also suffered through a couple school years working as a home PC installs contractor for a major electronics store. This was during the first Vista rollouts, which is to say that the work sucked considerably (though marginally better than scrubbing dishes at the dining hall).. That was rough, but nowhere else will you be taught more about the plight of the end user, customer service, and core workstation support.

At the end of it, all recruiters look at these days is a four year degree with a clean background who can navigate a few interviews. You'll be trained at whatever you need at the job. Where you'll come ahead of the crowd is having prior experience and practical skills, which will mean you might actually lead a successful career, as opposed to some of my no-value-added classmates.
